summary: This article examines how social media affects adolescent mental health, framing it as a double-edged sword that offers connection but also risks like cyberbullying, isolation and low self-esteem. It cites experts and studies from autumn 2023 and offers guidance for parents and educators on spotting distress, digital literacy, boundaries, role modeling, open communication, professional help, resilience and healthy habits.
one_line: An October 2023 overview of social media's effects on teen mental health, with expert advice for parents and educators on warning signs and prevention.
key_facts: The article was published for Mental Health Awareness month in October 2023.
A survey conducted between September and November 2023 showed a correlation between screen time and anxiety levels among young people.
Dr. Emily Thompson, a leading child psychologist, published research in the "Journal of Adolescent Health" on October 15, 2023.
Dr. Thompson's research found that teenagers who spend more than three hours per day on social media are more susceptible to internalizing behaviors such as withdrawal, anxiety, and depression.

Amy Green, a high school counselor in Springfield, advises parents to watch for out-of-character changes such as long hours online, secrecy about online activities, or loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities.

Tech educator Mark Johnson said at a digital wellness seminar on September 22, 2023 that teaching young people to be discerning content creators and consumers is as important as teaching them to cross the road safely.
On September 30, 2023, the "Parents for Safe Media" group held a workshop recommending time limits on app usage, regular discussions about online experiences, and "tech-free" zones or times at home.
Psychologist Dr. Raj Singh said in an October 5, 2023 webinar that adults should model moderate social media use, active engagement in the physical world, and healthy offline coping strategies.
A Family Online Safety Institute study published October 10, 2023 found that teens comfortable reporting negative online interactions to parents were less likely to experience prolonged distress.
Mental health professional Laura Schneider advises seeking a licensed therapist if a teen shows signs of depression or anxiety linked to social media interactions.
The article recommends building resilience through a growth mindset, real-life connections, and hobbies and talents outside the online sphere.
Healthy habits recommended include physical activity, face-to-face interactions, and adequate sleep, which excessive screen time can compromise.
